extracted.intended_audience: general readers and learners interested in communication and conversational skills
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, properties, and practical guidance for human conversation: definitions, when an interaction counts as conversation, etiquette/cooperative rules, conversational forms (banter, discussion, small talk), and related phenomena (narcissism, AI Turing test, intrapersonal talk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum definition of conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation is interactive communication between two or more people; no generally accepted definition beyond at least two people talking together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term is often defined by what it is not: ritualized exchanges (e.g., mutual greeting), interactions with a marked status differential (e.g., a boss giving orders), or interactions with a tightly focused topic or purpose are generally not considered conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informality, symmetry, and social-tie function
rubrics_metrics.description: "Conversation is the kind of speech that happens informally, symmetrically, and for the purposes of establishing and maintaining social ties."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From less technical perspectives: polite give-and-take among people talking for company. Usefulness: distinguishes conversation from negotiation/command styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow rules of etiquette / cooperative principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversations follow rules of etiquette because they depend on social convention; specific rules arise from the cooperative principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to adhere to these rules causes the conversation to deteriorate or end. Contributions should be responses to what has previously been said.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose medium by communicative ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversations may be optimal when parties desire relatively equal exchange or to build social ties; other media may be preferable when permanence or time-efficiency is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If permanency is important, written communication may be ideal; if time-efficient communication most important, a speech may be preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synchronous, face-to-face norm and nonverbal importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation is generally face-to-face person-to-person at the same time (synchronous); may include video/audio calls but generally not asynchronous written internet communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In face-to-face conversation much meaning is non-verbal/body language (the article cites ~85%); short forms like SMS are frequently misunderstood because they lack nonverbal cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banter: form and goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Banter is short witty sentences that bounce back and forth; often uses clever put-downs, witty insults, misunderstandings, zingers, flirtation, and puns; each line should 'top' the one before it and be a verbal war of wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important factors: subtext, situation, and rapport. Each line should evoke emotional response and ownership without hurting feelings. Maintain a structure/progression understood by parties; quit bantering with sensibility and avoid obsessing on topping each other. 'Brevity is the soul of wit.' Examples include film dialogues; storytelling methods: unexpected turns, intentional misunderstandings, layering anchors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banter delivery constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Every line in banter should be able to evoke both an emotional response and ownership without hurting one's feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a certain level of progression connecting the parties; methods include interrupting comfortable structure, taking the conversation toward crude form with evoking questions, or layering patterns. End banter before it becomes harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion vs dispute management
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion is sharing opinions on subjects thought of during conversation; in polite society the subject changes before discussion becomes dispute or controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid insisting a particular view be accepted when a topic risks becoming a dispute (example: theology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject categories to structure content
rubrics_metrics.description: Many conversations divide into four categories by major subject content: subjective ideas, objective facts, other people (usually absent), and oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proportional distribution among these categories offers psychological insights; few conversations fall exclusively into one category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional conversation vs small talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional conversation is designed to convey information to help achieve a goal; small talk values social purpose (bonding, managing personal distance) over topic importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of small talk: 'how is the weather' functions to bond rather than convey practical information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational narcissism: shift-response vs support-response
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversational narcissism is the tendency to steer conversation toward oneself; Derber distinguishes 'shift-response' (takes focus away from last speaker) from 'support-response' (maintains focus on the last speaker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer support-responses to avoid appearing self-centered; example: Shift-response — 'John: I'm feeling starved.' 'Mary: Oh, I just ate.' Support-response — 'John: I'm feeling starved.' 'Mary: When was the last time you ate?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual vulnerability between strangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain travel or transient situations produce strangers sharing intimate personal information they would not ordinarily share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special case: if one traveler is a mental health professional, the other may disclose in apparent hope of receiving help — be aware of ethical/contextual implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI conversational indistinguishability (Turing test) as evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: One test of AI conversational success is whether generated conversation cannot be distinguished from a human participant in text (the Turing test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitation: the Turing test conversation is by text not speech, so tone and nonverbal cues are not assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrapersonal conversation usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversing with oneself (intrapersonal communication) can help solve problems or serve therapeutic purposes like avoiding silence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize internal dialogue as a valid form of conversational processing and problem solving.
